newsitem.title: UK: IOSCO sees few differences on market surveillance.
newsitem.headline: IOSCO sees few differences on market surveillance.

text.p: The International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) sees few differences between markets and regulators over views on surveillance and contract design, Robert Wilmouth, Deputy Chairman of an IOSCO consultative Committee said.

IOSCO formed a sub-committee to provide a market perspective on work being carried out following last November's London summit between commodity market regulators and representatives from 17 countries.
"Our survey pointed out that there are not many differences between responses from exchanges and the regulators," Wilmouth said at the International Derivatives Conference.
The IOSCO sub-committee consisted of 10 representatives from futures exchanges and regulators from seven countries.
However, the IOSCO group cautioned against developing detailed 'best practice' design standards for commodity contracts, he said.

"We disagree with the London Communique's premise(issued after the November 1996 meeting) that physical delivery contracts based on physical commodities require more stringent standards and more intrusive involvement of a commodity market's supervisory regulator in the design process than cash-settled contracts," Wilmouth said.

A contract should be designed with the objective of not being readily susceptible to manipulation. However, it is more efficient to evaluate whether a contract can be manipulated once it has begun trading.
Meanwhile, co-ordinated monitoring of related positions across markets, although desirable, is not necessary, as each commodity market should be responsible for monitoring its own positions.
And if there are abusive practices, the deterrent should lie in the hands of the exchanges also.
"The primary responsibility for enforcement action should lie with the market authority closest to the conduct," Wilmouth added.
Only in cases where violative conduct takes place outside the market's oversight or crosses national boundaries should the government regulator become involved, he said.
Regarding information-sharing, Wilmouth said laws in different countries that impede this should be changed and harmonised to ensure the free flow of information and preserving its confidentiality.
